sections.title: Women and Gender in Buddhism: Theory, Text, Practice
sections.description: This course takes as its point of departure questions of women’s roles in Buddhist thought and practice, with a primary focus on women’s monastic orders. The history of the female monastic order (bhikkhunī sangha), in turn, opens onto the diverse, ambivalent, and contested roles women have taken in Buddhist institutions. More broadly, these concerns reflect the ways in which gender and sexuality have been theorized in Buddhist texts, traditions, and practices. To investigate these themes, the course begins with an introduction to the development of the bhikkhuni order. Why were women initially excluded from the Buddhist monkhood (sangha)? What doctrinal and practical amendments had to be made to allow for women’s ordination? Why did the order die out in some cases? From the development of the bhikkhuni order as recorded in early Buddhist literature, we turn to constructions of gender in Buddhist texts and practice, examining Buddhist masculinities and motherhood. We then turn to case studies of women’s monastic orders across Buddhist traditions, times, and places, investigating how doctrine and philosophy interact with lived reality. Case studies will be drawn primarily from Theravada traditions of South and Southeast Asia, but we will also consider doctrine and practice as related to women’s roles in East Asian and Tibetan Buddhist traditions. Buddhism is multivocal far more than monolithic, and part of the aim of this course is to show how there is no single approach to gender and sexuality, even within what might seem like a single tradition. Along the way, our discussions will open onto themes including: sexuality, celibacy and monasticism; representations of the feminine in Buddhist literature; Buddhist masculinities; motherhood; gender normativity and dis/ability; perspectives of queer, trans and nonbinary Buddhists; non-duality and not-self. We will explore these themes through close reading and analysis of texts as well as other media including music, film, artwork, and material culture. Experiential and participatory learning will also be important as we attend to the practices—such as meditation, chanting, pilgrimage, art-making, and more—that Buddhists undertake in the case studies we encounter.
